subject: Urban Planning
title: Highways Through Black Neighborhoods
description: A micro-lesson that makes Highways Through Black Neighborhoods usable.

hook.text: Interstate highways destroyed 475,000 homes in the US. A disproportionate number were in Black communities.

buildup.text: Highway planners in the 1950s-60s routed roads through Black business districts because land was cheap and resistance was weak.

discovery.text: Overtown in Miami, Black Bottom in Detroit, and Rondo in St. Paul were all thriving — then a highway arrived.

twist.text: Federal law required 'relocation assistance' but it was rarely provided. Displaced families received almost nothing.

climax.text: The Biden administration allocated $1 billion in 2021 to reconnect communities divided by highways.

punchline.text: Highways didn't just move through neighborhoods. They erased them.

quiz.question: Why were highways often routed through Black neighborhoods?
options: Those areas had the flattest terrain for road construction
Land was cheaper and political resistance was weaker there
Federal regulations required routes through urban centers
